## 1. The Forward Process

*How a fixed chain turns data into noise*

A diffusion model corrupts its data with a fixed Markov chain and then learns to undo the corruption. This module builds the chain: the one-step transition, the closed form that makes training cheap, the posterior the reverse process is matched against, and the signal-to-noise ratio that measures how far the corruption has gone.

**Learning outcomes**

- Write the forward transition and the closed form for q(x_t | x_0)
- Derive the posterior q(x_{t−1} | x_t, x_0) and explain why it is tractable
- Compute the signal-to-noise ratio at any step and say what it means
- Explain why the closed form and the Markov chain agree

### Lesson 1. What a diffusion model is

*A fixed corruption, and a learned undoing of it*

*Estimated study time:* 18 minutes

**What you will learn**

- State the two processes that make up a diffusion model
- Say what the "diffusion" is named after
- Explain why the forward process has no learnable parameters

**The ideas**

- A diffusion model is a latent variable model whose approximate posterior is fixed.
- The forward process adds Gaussian noise on a schedule; the reverse process learns to undo it.
- The prior at the end of the chain is the standard normal, so sampling starts from noise.

#### Practice

**Q. Which part of a diffusion model has learnable parameters? — multiple-choice *(warmup)***

- The forward process
- ✓ **The reverse process**
- The variance schedule
- The prior

> Correct — the reverse process mean is produced by the network.

> **Why:** The forward process and the schedule are fixed by hand. Everything the model learns lives in the reverse process, whose mean is a function of the noisy state and the timestep.

**Q. The forward process gradually destroys the information in the data. — boolean *(warmup)***

> **Answer:** True

> **Why:** Yes. The signal-to-noise ratio falls monotonically, and by the last step the state is essentially the prior, carrying almost no information about the data.

#### Go and do it

Step a data point through the forward chain and watch the signal disappear. Open **Watch the chain run** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §2 Background · p. 3 — The reverse process of equation 1, the forward process of equation 2, and the variational bound of equation 3.
- §1 Introduction · p. 1 — The description of the model as a parameterised Markov chain trained with variational inference.

**Further reading**

- [Ho, Jain & Abbeel, arXiv:2006.11239](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239) — The primary source.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Diffusion model** — A generative model that learns to reverse a fixed noise-addition process.
- **Forward process** — The fixed chain that adds noise to the data.
- **Reverse process** — The learned chain that removes noise.
- **Variance schedule** — The sequence β_1 … β_T that sets how much noise each step adds.

### Lesson 2. The closed form

*Sampling any timestep in one step*

*Estimated study time:* 22 minutes

**What you will learn**

- State q(x_t | x_0) and derive it from the one-step transition
- Explain why the closed form is what makes diffusion training affordable
- Verify that the closed form and the Markov chain describe the same distribution

**The ideas**

- x_t = √ᾱ_t · x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε, with ε ~ N(0, I).
- The state is a scaled copy of the data plus a scaled copy of a noise vector.
- Training never unrolls the chain: one timestep, one noise draw, one network evaluation.

#### Practice

**Q. The closed form q(x_t | x_0) has the form x_t = √ᾱ_t · x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε. What is ε? — multiple-choice *(warmup)***

- ✓ **A standard normal vector**
- The previous state x_{t−1}
- A learnable parameter
- The posterior mean

> Correct: ε ~ N(0, I), drawn fresh at every training step.

> **Why:** ε is a standard normal draw, and it is the same vector that the network is trained to predict. That is the whole trick: the target of the training objective is a random vector the model never has to see.

**Q. With the paper’s linear schedule, β goes from 10⁻⁴ to 0.02 over 1000 steps. What is β at the first step? — numeric *(core)***

> **Answer:** 0.0001 β_1

> **Why:** β_1 = 10⁻⁴ exactly. The schedule is linear in the step index, so the first and last values are the endpoints of the range.

#### Go and do it

Compare the two ways of reaching the same timestep. Open **Check the closed form against the chain** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §2 Background · p. 4 — Equation 4, the closed form q(x_t | x_0), and the statement that efficient training follows from it.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **ᾱ (alpha bar)** — The cumulative product of the α_t, so ᾱ_t = ∏ α_s.
- **Signal-to-noise ratio** — ᾱ_t divided by 1 − ᾱ_t: how much signal survives against how much noise.
- **Marginal** — The distribution of one timestep, with the intermediate steps summed out.

*Read first:* What a diffusion model is

### Lesson 3. The posterior

*The one quantity that has to be tractable*

*Estimated study time:* 20 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Write the posterior q(x_{t−1} | x_t, x_0)
- Explain why a tractable posterior is what makes the variational bound usable
- Compute the posterior mean and variance for a given step

**The ideas**

- q(x_{t−1} | x_t, x_0) is Gaussian, and so is the reverse process it is compared against.
- Every KL term in the bound therefore has a closed form instead of a Monte Carlo estimate.
- The posterior leans on x_0 at small t and on x_t at large t.

#### Practice

**Q. Why does the paper need q(x_{t−1} | x_t, x_0) to have a closed form? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **So every KL term in the bound can be computed between two Gaussians**
- So the sampling can be done in one step
- So the model does not need a network
- So the data can be scaled to [−1, 1]

> Correct.

> **Why:** The variational bound is a sum of KL divergences between the true posterior and the model’s reverse transition. If both are Gaussian, each term has a closed form instead of a high-variance Monte Carlo estimate.

#### Go and do it

See the posterior shift its weight from x_0 to x_t as the noise grows. Open **Move the posterior weight** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §2 Background · p. 4 — Equations 6 and 7: the posterior mean and the posterior variance β̃_t.
- §2 Background · p. 3 — Equation 5: the decomposition of the bound into per-step KL terms.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Posterior** — q(x_{t−1} | x_t, x_0): where the chain would have been, given the data.
- **Variational bound** — An upper bound on the negative log likelihood, decomposed into per-step KL terms.
- **KL divergence** — A measure of how far one distribution is from another.

*Read first:* The closed form

## 2. The Reverse Process

*Learning to walk the corruption backwards*

The reverse process is a Markov chain of learned Gaussians. This module derives the ε-prediction parameterisation, the two other standard parameterisations, the ancestral sampler, and the deterministic sampler that makes diffusion models fast.

**Learning outcomes**

- Derive the ε-prediction parameterisation from the variational bound
- Convert between ε-prediction, x₀-prediction and v-prediction
- Run the ancestral sampler and the deterministic sampler
- State what the training objective actually optimises, and what it gives up

### Lesson 4. The training objective

*Why predicting the noise is the same as predicting the score*

*Estimated study time:* 26 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Derive the ε-prediction parameterisation from the bound
- State the simplified objective and what it gives up
- Explain the connection to denoising score matching

**The ideas**

- The reverse mean can be written in terms of a network that predicts ε.
- With that parameterisation the bound becomes a weighted squared error on ε.
- Dropping the weight gives the objective the paper actually uses.

#### Practice

**Q. With the ε-prediction parameterisation, the network is trained to predict… — multiple-choice *(core)***

- the clean sample x_0
- ✓ **the noise ε that was added**
- the posterior mean μ̃_t
- the reverse variance σ_t

> Correct.

> **Why:** Predicting ε makes the bound resemble denoising score matching and makes the sampler resemble Langevin dynamics. Both facts are the paper’s stated reasons for preferring it.

**Q. In the simplified objective the weight on the loss is exactly what value at every timestep? — numeric *(core)***

> **Answer:** 1

> **Why:** Exactly 1. The true bound weights the loss by β_t² / (2 σ_t² α_t (1 − ᾱ_t)); the simplified objective replaces that whole factor with 1, which is why it down-weights small t so dramatically.

#### Go and do it

Compare the weight of the true bound with the flat weight of the simplified objective. Open **See the weight the simplification drops** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §3.2 Reverse process and L_{1:T−1} · p. 7 — Equations 8 to 12: from the KL term to the ε-prediction parameterisation of equation 11 and the weighted loss of equation 12.
- §3.4 Simplified training objective · p. 10 — Equation 14, the simplified objective, and the reason the small-t terms are down-weighted.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **ε-prediction** — Parameterising the reverse mean through a network that predicts the added noise.
- **Score** — The gradient of the log density with respect to the input.
- **Denoising score matching** — Training a score network by asking it to predict the noise that was added.
- **Simplified objective** — The unweighted squared error on ε that the paper actually trains with.

*Read first:* The posterior

### Lesson 5. Three parameterisations

*ε, x₀, and v*

*Estimated study time:* 18 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Convert a prediction in one parameterisation into another
- State which parameterisation the paper found best and why
- Predict what changes when the network predicts x₀ instead of ε

**The ideas**

- The three parameterisations describe the same reverse process; only the network target changes.
- Predicting x₀ is unstable at large t, where the estimate of x₀ is dominated by noise.
- The v-prediction is the reparameterisation that interpolates between them.

#### Practice

**Q. Which statement about the three parameterisations is true? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- They define three different reverse processes
- ✓ **They describe the same reverse process but train the network on different targets**
- Only ε-prediction is mathematically valid
- x₀-prediction is always better

> Correct.

> **Why:** The three parameterisations are algebraically equivalent views of p_θ(x_{t−1}|x_t). What changes is the regression target, and therefore how stable training is and how the loss is weighted.

#### Go and do it

Take one network output and read it as ε, as x₀, and as v. Open **Convert a prediction** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §3.2 Reverse process and L_{1:T−1} · p. 8 — The remark that predicting x_0 led to worse sample quality early on, and the summary of the two parameterisations.
- §4.2 Reverse process parameterization and training objective ablation · p. 12 — Table 2: the measured comparison of the two parameterisations under both objectives.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **v-prediction** — Predicting the velocity √ᾱ_t ε − √(1−ᾱ_t) x_0.
- **x₀-prediction** — Parameterising the reverse mean through a network that predicts the clean sample.

*Read first:* The training objective

### Lesson 6. Sampling

*From noise to a sample, and back again*

*Estimated study time:* 24 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Run the ancestral sampler and account for the noise it adds
- Explain what a deterministic sampler does differently
- Describe the cost of sampling in network evaluations

**The ideas**

- The ancestral sampler adds σ_t · z at every step.
- A deterministic sampler reuses the same noise and can be run in fewer steps.
- Sampling is the expensive half: T network evaluations per sample.

#### Practice

**Q. Sampling with T = 1000 steps needs one network evaluation per step. How many network evaluations does a single sample cost? — numeric *(warmup)***

> **Answer:** 1000

> **Why:** Exactly 1000. This is the cost the paper notes it shares with earlier work, and it is the reason every later improvement in this area is about taking fewer steps.

**Q. What does a deterministic sampler change? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **It removes the fresh noise, so the same start gives the same sample**
- It removes the network from the loop
- It replaces the variance schedule with a learned one
- It trains the model with a different objective

> Correct.

> **Why:** DDIM removes the fresh noise at each step, turning the reverse chain into a probability-flow ODE. The same latent then always gives the same sample, which is what allows the number of steps to be cut without collapsing diversity.

#### Go and do it

Sample from a trained model and watch the trajectory back to the data. Open **Run the reverse chain** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §3.2 Reverse process and L_{1:T−1} · p. 8 — Algorithm 2, the sampling procedure, and the remark that it resembles Langevin dynamics.
- §3.4 Simplified training objective · p. 10 — Algorithm 1, the training procedure.

**Further reading**

- [Song, Meng & Ermon, arXiv:2010.02502](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502) — DDIM: the deterministic sampler.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Ancestral sampling** — The sampler that adds fresh noise at every reverse step.
- **DDIM** — A deterministic sampler for the same trained model.
- **Deterministic sampler** — A sampler that adds no fresh noise, so the same starting point gives the same sample.

*Read first:* Three parameterisations

## 3. Noise Schedules

*Choosing how fast the signal disappears*

The schedule is the one set of choices in the model that is not learned. This module compares the linear schedule of the original paper with the cosine schedule that followed, and shows what the schedule does to the training signal.

**Learning outcomes**

- Compare the linear and cosine schedules on the same number of steps
- Explain the effect of a schedule on the terminal KL divergence
- Compute the weight the true variational bound puts on each timestep
- Argue for a schedule choice from the signal-to-noise ratio alone

### Lesson 7. Choosing a schedule

*Linear, cosine, and what they do to the signal*

*Estimated study time:* 20 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Write the linear schedule of the original paper
- Explain what the schedule controls
- Compute the terminal KL divergence for a given schedule

**The ideas**

- The paper fixes β to grow linearly from 1e-4 to 0.02 over T = 1000 steps.
- The schedule is the only part of the model that is not learned.
- A good schedule spends its steps where the denoising task is informative.

#### Practice

**Q. What does the variance schedule control? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **How much noise each step adds, and therefore the whole signal-to-noise trajectory**
- The size of the network
- The learning rate
- The resolution of the images

> Correct.

> **Why:** The schedule determines ᾱ_t at every step, and therefore the signal-to-noise ratio, the terminal KL divergence, and the weighting of the training objective.

**Q. The paper quotes a terminal KL divergence of about 10⁻⁵ bits per dimension for its linear schedule. Roughly how many bits per dimension is that, in scientific notation? — numeric *(hard)***

> **Answer:** 0.00001 ± 1e-7

> **Why:** 10⁻⁵ bits per dimension. The point of the number is that x_T is, for every practical purpose, indistinguishable from the prior — which is what lets the sampler start from pure noise.

#### Go and do it

Put the linear and cosine schedules side by side and read the signal-to-noise ratio off each. Open **Compare two schedules** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §4 Experiments · p. 11 — T = 1000, β linear from 1e-4 to 0.02, and the quoted terminal KL of roughly 1e-5 bits per dimension.
- §3.1 Forward process and L_T · p. 6 — The reason the forward variances are fixed rather than learned: the terminal term is then a constant.

**Further reading**

- [Nichol & Dhariwal, arXiv:2102.09672](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.09672) — The cosine schedule and learned variances.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Variance schedule** — The sequence β_1 … β_T that sets how much noise each step adds.
- **Terminal KL** — How far the final noisy state is from the standard normal prior.

*Read first:* The closed form

### Lesson 8. The weighting

*Why the simplified objective is not the same objective*

*Estimated study time:* 18 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Write the weight of the true variational bound at each timestep
- Explain the consequence of dropping the weight
- Say what the paper gives up when it uses the simplified objective

**The ideas**

- The true bound weights the loss by β_t² / (2 σ_t² α_t (1 − ᾱ_t)).
- That weight is enormous at small t and tiny at large t.
- The simplified objective flattens it, so small t is effectively ignored.

#### Practice

**Q. Dropping the weight from the true variational bound has which effect? — multiple-choice *(hard)***

- ✓ **Small t are effectively ignored, because the true weight there is enormous**
- Large t are ignored
- The objective becomes a different likelihood bound
- Nothing changes, because the weight is constant

> Correct.

> **Why:** The true weight β_t²/(2σ_t²α_t(1−ᾱ_t)) is very large at small t and very small at large t. Flattening it to 1 therefore removes most of the gradient signal from the easy, small-t end of the chain — which the paper reports improves sample quality.

#### Go and do it

Break the bound into its per-step KL terms and see where the cost sits. Open **Decompose the bound** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §3.4 Simplified training objective · p. 10 — The statement that the simplified objective down-weights the loss terms corresponding to small t.
- §4.1 Sample quality · p. 11 — Table 1: the true bound gives better codelengths, the simplified objective gives better samples.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Variational bound** — An upper bound on the negative log likelihood, decomposed into per-step KL terms.
- **Simplified objective** — The unweighted squared error on ε that the paper actually trains with.

*Read first:* The training objective, Choosing a schedule

## 4. Latent Diffusion

*Why the diffusion happens in someone else’s space*

Rombach et al. did not improve the diffusion model; they moved it into an autoencoder’s latent space. This module measures the compression, the reconstruction error it costs, and the scaling factor that makes the latents behave like the data the schedule assumes.

**Learning outcomes**

- Compute the saving a latent diffusion model buys, in elements and in attention
- Measure the reconstruction error a compression buys
- Explain why the latents have to be rescaled
- Trace what happens to the signal-to-noise ratio in the latent space

### Lesson 9. The latent space

*Moving the diffusion into an autoencoder*

*Estimated study time:* 20 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Compute the reduction in elements and in attention a compression buys
- Measure the reconstruction error a compression costs
- Explain the role of the scaling factor

**The ideas**

- A diffusion model in pixel space wastes most of its capacity on high frequencies.
- An autoencoder moves the problem into a lower dimensional space, and the saving is roughly quadratic.
- The latents have to be rescaled, because the schedule assumes unit-variance data.

#### Practice

**Q. Why does latent diffusion use an autoencoder at all? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **The diffusion runs on far fewer elements, so it is much cheaper**
- The autoencoder makes the images sharper
- It removes the need for a variance schedule
- It allows the model to be trained on text

> Correct.

> **Why:** Compressing by a factor f reduces the number of elements by roughly 1/f² and the attention cost by roughly 1/f⁴, because attention is quadratic in the number of tokens.

**Q. An autoencoder compresses a 256×256 image with 3 channels by a factor of 8, to 4 latent channels. By what factor is the number of elements the diffusion model works on reduced? — numeric *(hard)***

> **Answer:** 48

> **Why:** The image has 256×256×3 = 196,608 elements; the latent has 32×32×4 = 4,096. The reduction factor is 48. The attention saving is larger still, because it is quadratic in the token count.

#### Go and do it

Train a real autoencoder and watch the reconstruction error against the compression ratio. Open **Measure the compression** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §2 Background · p. 3 — The argument that the top-level latent x_T has nearly zero mutual information with the data.

**Further reading**

- [Rombach et al., arXiv:2112.10752](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752) — Latent diffusion, and the scaling factor of 0.18215.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Latent diffusion** — Running the diffusion in an autoencoder’s latent space instead of in pixel space.
- **Autoencoder** — A learned encoder and decoder pair that compresses data and reconstructs it.
- **Scaling factor** — The constant that rescales the latents so they have roughly unit variance.

*Read first:* The closed form

## 5. Guidance

*Steering a generative model with a condition*

Guidance is how a diffusion model is made to obey a prompt. This module derives classifier-free guidance from the score, and measures the trade-off it buys: sharper samples, less diversity, and a model that is no longer sampling the distribution it was trained on.

**Learning outcomes**

- Write the guided score and explain each term
- Predict what a guidance weight does to fidelity and to diversity
- Derive the classifier-guided update and compare it with the classifier-free one
- Say precisely what a guided model is sampling

### Lesson 10. Classifier-free guidance

*Guiding without a classifier*

*Estimated study time:* 24 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Write the guided score
- Derive it from the conditional and unconditional scores
- Explain why the guided model is not sampling the training distribution

**The ideas**

- s_guided = s_uncond + w · (s_cond − s_uncond).
- The guided distribution is the training distribution tilted by p(c | x)^w.
- Raising w sharpens the samples and reduces their diversity.

#### Practice

**Q. The classifier-free guided score is s_uncond + w · (s_cond − s_uncond). What does w = 0 give? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **The unconditional score**
- The conditional score
- A score of zero
- The posterior mean

> Correct.

> **Why:** At w = 0 the guidance term vanishes and the sampler is unconditional. At w = 1 the guided score is exactly the conditional score.

**Q. What does a large guidance weight do to the samples? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **They cluster more tightly on the mode that matches the condition**
- They spread out to cover the tail of the distribution
- They become noisier
- They become independent of the condition

> Correct: sharper, but less diverse.

> **Why:** Guidance tilts the distribution by p(c|x)^w, which sharpens the conditional but suppresses everything else. The result is better prompt adherence and worse coverage — the classic fidelity–diversity trade-off.

#### Go and do it

Measure fidelity and diversity against the guidance weight, with an exact score. Open **Sweep the guidance weight** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Further reading**

- [Ho & Salimans, arXiv:2207.12598](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598) — The classifier-free guidance derivation.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Guidance** — Steering a generative model towards a condition by interpolating its scores.
- **Classifier-free guidance** — Guidance that needs no classifier, because the condition is dropped out during training.
- **Score** — The gradient of the log density with respect to the input.
- **Mode collapse** — A generator that produces only a subset of the data distribution.

*Read first:* The training objective

### Lesson 11. The price of guidance

*What the extra fidelity costs*

*Estimated study time:* 18 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Quantify the trade-off between fidelity and diversity
- Explain the relationship between guidance weight and the effective temperature
- Predict what a very large guidance weight does

**The ideas**

- Guidance narrows the distribution: the samples move to the mode and stop spreading.
- A large guidance weight behaves like a low temperature, but not exactly.
- The guided model has higher likelihood on some inputs and much lower on others.

#### Practice

**Q. A guided model samples from a distribution proportional to p(x) · p(c | x)^w. For what value of w is this distribution exactly p(x | c)? — numeric *(hard)***

> **Answer:** 1

> **Why:** w = 1. Since p(x)·p(c|x) = p(x|c)·p(c), and p(c) is a constant, the tilted distribution is proportional to the true conditional. Any w above 1 over-shoots it.

#### Go and do it

Put fidelity against diversity and mark where the sweet spot is. Open **Plot the trade-off** in the diffusion-lab application.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Mode collapse** — A generator that produces only a subset of the data distribution.
- **Guidance** — Steering a generative model towards a condition by interpolating its scores.

*Read first:* Classifier-free guidance

## 6. The Design Space

*The choices that survived*

The original paper fixed a dozen choices for convenience. Later work showed which of them mattered. This module covers the σ parametrisation, the preconditioning functions, the deterministic samplers, and the arithmetic of how many network evaluations a sample costs.

**Learning outcomes**

- Compare the timestep and σ parametrisations
- Explain what a preconditioning function is for
- Count the network evaluations a given number of steps costs
- Describe the difference between a stochastic and a deterministic sampler

### Lesson 12. The design space

*The choices that turned out to matter*

*Estimated study time:* 22 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Compare the timestep parametrisation with the σ parametrisation
- Explain what a preconditioning function does
- Count the network evaluations a sampler costs

**The ideas**

- The original paper fixed many choices for convenience; later work separated the ones that matter.
- Preconditioning decides how the loss at one noise level is weighted against the others.
- The number of steps is the only number that matters for sampling cost.

#### Practice

**Q. What is preconditioning for? — multiple-choice *(hard)***

- ✓ **Deciding how the loss at one noise level counts against the others**
- Choosing the number of sampling steps
- Rescaling the data to [−1, 1]
- Making the network smaller

> Correct.

> **Why:** Different noise levels have different intrinsic difficulty and different signal-to-noise ratios, so a single unweighted loss trains them badly. Preconditioning is the per-level weight that fixes this.

**Q. A sampler takes 50 steps out of a chain of length 1000. How many network evaluations does one sample cost? — numeric *(core)***

> **Answer:** 50

> **Why:** Exactly 50. The number of steps is the only thing that matters for sampling cost, which is why deterministic samplers that can be run in few steps matter so much.

#### Go and do it

Add up what a sample costs, in network evaluations and in memory. Open **Count the cost** in the diffusion-lab application.

**Further reading**

- [Karras et al., arXiv:2206.00364](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00364) — The σ parametrisation, the preconditioning functions and the design-space analysis.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Preconditioning** — A weighting that decides how the loss at one noise level counts against the others.
- **σ parametrisation** — Indexing the noise levels by the standard deviation of the data noise.

*Read first:* Sampling, Choosing a schedule

## Appendix A — Glossary

**Diffusion model** — A generative model that learns to reverse a fixed noise-addition process.

A diffusion model is a latent variable model with two parts: a forward process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to the data, and a reverse process, learned, that removes it. Because the forward process is fixed, the model has few enough degrees of freedom to train well and the resulting samples are competitive with GANs.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Forward process** — The fixed chain that adds noise to the data.

Also called the diffusion process. It is a Markov chain q(x_1:T | x_0) = ∏ q(x_t | x_{t−1}) in which each step multiplies the state by √α_t and adds Gaussian noise of scale √β_t. It has no learnable parameters at all.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Reverse process** — The learned chain that removes noise.

A Markov chain p_θ(x_{0:T}) = p(x_T) ∏ p_θ(x_{t−1} | x_t) whose transitions are Gaussians with learned means and fixed variances. The means are produced by a network that takes the noisy state and the timestep.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Variance schedule** — The sequence β_1 … β_T that sets how much noise each step adds.

The only unlearned choice in the model. The original paper fixes it to grow linearly from 1e-4 to 0.02 over 1000 steps. Later work found a cosine schedule to be better, and even allows the schedule itself to be learned.

*Example:* What are β_1 and β_T in the paper’s setup? → 10⁻⁴ and 0.02 respectively, with T = 1000 steps.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**ᾱ (alpha bar)** — The cumulative product of the α_t, so ᾱ_t = ∏ α_s.

ᾱ_t is the fraction of the original signal still present in x_t. It is the single most useful number in the whole model: it appears in the closed form for x_t, in the posterior, and in the weighting of the training objective.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Marginal** — The distribution of one timestep, with the intermediate steps summed out.

q(x_t | x_0) is the marginal of the forward chain at step t, with x_1 … x_{t−1} integrated out. Because the chain is Gaussian, that marginal is itself Gaussian, and it has a closed form.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Signal-to-noise ratio** — ᾱ_t divided by 1 − ᾱ_t: how much signal survives against how much noise.

The SNR of the forward process at step t. It is one above 1 while the data is still mostly intact and falls below 1 as the state becomes mostly noise. The schedule determines the whole trajectory of the SNR, and therefore which steps are worth training on.

*Example:* At what step does the SNR cross one? → Where ᾱ_t = 0.5. For the paper’s linear schedule over 1000 steps that is around t = 500.

*Course term*

**Posterior** — q(x_{t−1} | x_t, x_0): where the chain would have been, given the data.

The approximate posterior of the latent variable model. It is Gaussian, with a mean that is a fixed linear combination of x_0 and x_t, and a variance β̃_t. It is the target the reverse process is compared against, and its tractability is what makes the variational bound computable.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Variational bound** — An upper bound on the negative log likelihood, decomposed into per-step KL terms.

L = D_KL(q(x_T|x_0) ‖ p(x_T)) + Σ D_KL(q(x_{t−1}|x_t,x_0) ‖ p_θ(x_{t−1}|x_t)) − log p_θ(x_0|x_1). Every term compares two Gaussians, so every term has a closed form rather than needing a Monte Carlo estimate.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**KL divergence** — A measure of how far one distribution is from another.

D_KL(P ‖ Q) = ∫ P log(P/Q). Between two univariate Gaussians it has a closed form, which is why the diffusion bound is cheap to compute.

*Course term*

**ε-prediction** — Parameterising the reverse mean through a network that predicts the added noise.

μ_θ(x_t, t) = (1/√α_t)(x_t − (β_t/√(1−ᾱ_t)) ε_θ(x_t, t)). The paper argues for this parameterisation because it makes the bound look like denoising score matching and makes sampling look like Langevin dynamics.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**x₀-prediction** — Parameterising the reverse mean through a network that predicts the clean sample.

An alternative target for the same reverse process. The paper reports that it works only with the full variational bound, and that it leads to worse sample quality early in training.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**v-prediction** — Predicting the velocity √ᾱ_t ε − √(1−ᾱ_t) x_0.

A reparameterisation that interpolates between ε-prediction and x₀-prediction. It is numerically better behaved at high noise levels, and is used in several later systems.

*Course term*

**Score** — The gradient of the log density with respect to the input.

∇_x log p(x). A network that predicts the score of the noisy distribution at every noise level is a denoising score model, and sampling from it is annealed Langevin dynamics.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Denoising score matching** — Training a score network by asking it to predict the noise that was added.

The equivalence the paper leans on: optimising a weighted variational bound on a diffusion model is equivalent to training a score-based model with denoising score matching over multiple noise levels.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Simplified objective** — The unweighted squared error on ε that the paper actually trains with.

L_simple = E ‖ε − ε_θ(√ᾱ_t x_0 + √(1−ᾱ_t) ε, t)‖². It drops the weight of the true bound, which down-weights small t. The paper reports better codelengths from the true bound and better samples from the simplified one.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Ancestral sampling** — The sampler that adds fresh noise at every reverse step.

Algorithm 2 of the paper: x_{t−1} = (1/√α_t)(x_t − (β_t/√(1−ᾱ_t)) ε_θ) + σ_t z, with z ~ N(0, I) and z = 0 at the last step.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**DDIM** — A deterministic sampler for the same trained model.

Denoising diffusion implicit models rewrite the reverse chain so that the marginals are deterministic given x_0, turning sampling into an ODE that can be jumped over. η = 0 gives a fully deterministic sampler; η = 1 recovers the ancestral one.

*Song, Meng & Ermon (2021)*

**Deterministic sampler** — A sampler that adds no fresh noise, so the same starting point gives the same sample.

The same latent always produces the same output, which makes the samplers comparable and lets the number of steps be reduced without the loss of diversity that stochasticity would cause.

*Song, Meng & Ermon (2021)*

**Terminal KL** — How far the final noisy state is from the standard normal prior.

D_KL(q(x_T|x_0) ‖ N(0, I)). The paper quotes roughly 10⁻⁵ bits per dimension for its linear schedule, which is the statement that x_T carries essentially no information about the data.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Latent diffusion** — Running the diffusion in an autoencoder’s latent space instead of in pixel space.

The technique behind Stable Diffusion. The saving is roughly quadratic in the compression factor, because both the number of spatial positions and the number of channels shrink.

*Rombach et al. (2022)*

**Autoencoder** — A learned encoder and decoder pair that compresses data and reconstructs it.

In latent diffusion the autoencoder is usually a convolutional one trained separately. Its reconstruction error is the price paid for the compression.

*Rombach et al. (2022)*

**Scaling factor** — The constant that rescales the latents so they have roughly unit variance.

The forward process assumes data with unit-ish variance. Rombach et al. multiply their latents by 0.18215 to achieve that, and the choice matters: without it the schedule is mismatched to the data.

*Rombach et al. (2022)*

**Guidance** — Steering a generative model towards a condition by interpolating its scores.

The guided score is a linear combination of the unconditional and the conditional score, with a weight that decides how far to go. Guidance is what makes a text-to-image model obey its prompt.

*Ho & Salimans (2022)*

**Classifier-free guidance** — Guidance that needs no classifier, because the condition is dropped out during training.

s_guided = s_uncond + w(s_cond − s_uncond). The model is trained both with and without the condition, so the two scores come from the same network. It is simpler than classifier guidance and works better in practice.

*Ho & Salimans (2022)*

**Mode collapse** — A generator that produces only a subset of the data distribution.

Guidance causes a specific kind of it: the samples concentrate on the mode that matches the condition and stop covering the rest of the distribution.

*Course term*

**Preconditioning** — A weighting that decides how the loss at one noise level counts against the others.

Different noise levels have different intrinsic difficulty, so the loss has to be scaled per level for the network to be trained well. The design-space paper treats this as a function of σ and t rather than of the raw loss.

*Karras et al. (2022)*

**σ parametrisation** — Indexing the noise levels by the standard deviation of the data noise.

An alternative to indexing by timestep, in which the model is written in terms of σ, the noise level itself. It makes the design space easier to reason about and is the basis of several later samplers.

*Karras et al. (2022)*

**Rate–distortion** — A view of the generative model as a lossy compressor.

The bound’s KL terms are the rate; the reconstruction error is the distortion. The paper reports that more than half of a diffusion model’s lossless codelength describes imperceptible detail.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Progressive generation** — Large-scale structure appears first and fine detail last.

Predicting x̂_0 from a noisy x_t at each step of the reverse chain gives a sequence of ever sharper estimates. Large features are decided early, details late.

*Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)*

**Noise swap** — Replacing the noise in a noisy sample to see what the model kept.

Taking x_t from one data point and rebuilding it with the noise from another isolates structure from texture, with no model involved at all.

*Course term*

**Signal** — The part of x_t that comes from the data rather than from the noise.

In x_t = √ᾱ_t x_0 + √(1−ᾱ_t) ε, the first term is the signal and the second is the noise. Their ratio is the signal-to-noise ratio, and it is the single number that describes how corrupted the state is.

*Course term*

## 1. Superposition

*Why a dimension has to hold more than one thing*

When a model has fewer dimensions than the features it wants to represent, something has to give. This module builds the toy model in which that something is computable, and measures the interference that follows.

**Learning outcomes**

- State the linear toy model and the loss it optimises
- Compute the interference between two features that share a direction
- Explain what the importance threshold is and why it exists

### Lesson 1. The toy model

*A model with fewer dimensions than features*

*Estimated study time:* 24 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Write the linear toy model and the loss it minimises
- Derive the expected squared error of one feature
- Explain what the interference term is

**The ideas**

- The loss of one feature is 1 − 2‖w_k‖² + Σ_m (w_k·w_m)².
- When the columns are orthonormal, what is left is pure interference.
- Interference is the price of putting two features in one direction.

#### Practice

**Q. What does superposition force a model to do? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **Pack several features into one direction**
- Drop the features it cannot represent
- Make the features more important
- Use more dimensions

> Correct.

> **Why:** With fewer dimensions than features, the columns cannot all be orthogonal, so some features share a direction and interfere with each other.

**Q. Two features share a direction, and the squared projection of one onto the other is 0.25. What is the interference term in the loss? — numeric *(core)***

> **Answer:** 0.25

> **Why:** The cross term is (w_i·w_j)², so the interference is the square of the projection: 0.25.

#### Go and do it

Fit the toy model at a given number of dimensions and read the interference. Open **Fit the model** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §sae:2 Taking Features out of Superposition with Sparse Dictionary Learning · p. 2 — The toy model of superposition that the sparse-autoencoder paper is built on, and the interference it costs.

**Further reading**

- [A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework.html) — The vocabulary of the residual stream, nodes, edges and paths.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Superposition** — Several features packed into one direction of the model’s activation.
- **Interference** — The cost two features pay for sharing a direction.
- **Importance** — How much a feature matters to the loss.

### Lesson 2. The importance threshold

*When a feature is not worth representing*

*Estimated study time:* 20 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Explain why the model drops some features and keeps others
- Measure the threshold at which a feature starts to be represented
- Say what happens to the interference as the tail is dropped

**The ideas**

- Hosting a feature costs the host; dropping it costs the feature itself.
- The threshold is where those two prices cross.
- A power law of importances produces a sharp threshold.

#### Practice

**Q. Why does a model drop some features? — multiple-choice *(hard)***

- ✓ **Because hosting them would cost the host more than dropping them costs them**
- Because they do not fit
- Because they are noisy
- It never does

> Correct.

> **Why:** Hosting a feature costs the host the interference; dropping it costs the feature its own importance. The threshold is where those cross.

#### Go and do it

Sweep a feature’s importance and watch the model decide whether to keep it. Open **Find the threshold** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §sae:2 Taking Features out of Superposition with Sparse Dictionary Learning · p. 3 — The importance threshold, and the argument that the tail of the importance distribution is not worth representing.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Importance** — How much a feature matters to the loss.
- **Interference** — The cost two features pay for sharing a direction.
- **Polysemanticity** — A neuron that responds to several unrelated things.

*Read first:* The toy model

## 2. Features, Not Neurons

*A neuron is a mixture; a feature is not*

The central observation of mechanistic interpretability: individual neurons are polysemantic, and the features a model represents do not line up with the neurons it uses to represent them. This module unpacks that, and builds the tool that fixes it.

**Learning outcomes**

- Explain polysemanticity and why it is a problem
- Write the sparse autoencoder and its objective
- Measure the sparsity, the reconstruction and the interpretability of a dictionary

### Lesson 3. Polysemanticity

*Why a neuron is not a feature*

*Estimated study time:* 20 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Define polysemanticity
- Explain why superposition makes it unavoidable
- Say what a monosemantic feature would look like

**The ideas**

- A neuron that responds to several things is polysemantic.
- Superposition makes polysemantic neurons the cheap option.
- A feature is a thing the model represents, not a neuron it represents it with.

#### Practice

**Q. A neuron in a superposed model is usually polysemantic. — boolean *(core)***

> **Answer:** True

> **Why:** Yes. Superposition is what makes it cheap for one neuron to respond to several things, so polysemantic neurons are the cheap option rather than a failure.

#### Go and do it

Count how many features each direction is carrying. Open **How many features per direction** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §sae:1 Introduction · p. 1 — The problem: a neuron responds to several things, and the features a model represents are not the neurons it uses.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Polysemanticity** — A neuron that responds to several unrelated things.
- **Monosemanticity** — A direction that responds to one thing and nothing else.
- **Feature** — A thing the model represents, as distinct from the neuron it uses.

*Read first:* The importance threshold

### Lesson 4. The sparse autoencoder

*Asking for a sparse code*

*Estimated study time:* 24 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Write the encoder, the decoder and the objective of a sparse autoencoder
- Explain what the sparsity penalty is for
- Measure the reconstruction, the sparsity and the explained variance

**The ideas**

- The autoencoder asks for a code that is sparse and reconstructs.
- The L1 penalty is what makes the code sparse.
- A dictionary feature that activates for one thing is interpretable.

#### Practice

**Q. What is the L1 penalty in a sparse autoencoder for? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **To make the code sparse**
- To make the reconstruction better
- To make the dictionary larger
- To make the training faster

> Correct.

> **Why:** The L1 term penalises the number of active features, and the sparsity is what makes a dictionary feature correspond to one thing.

**Q. A sparse autoencoder reconstructs activations with a mean squared error of 0.1, and the activations have variance 0.8. What is the explained variance? — numeric *(hard)***

> **Answer:** 0.875 ± 0.001

> **Why:** 1 − 0.1/0.8 = 0.875. The dictionary has kept most of the information.

#### Go and do it

Train a real sparse autoencoder on a real residual stream and watch it find features. Open **Train the autoencoder** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §sae:2 Taking Features out of Superposition with Sparse Dictionary Learning · p. 4 — The encoder, the decoder, the sparsity penalty, and the objective.
- §sae:3 Interpreting Dictionary Features · p. 5 — How a dictionary feature is scored, and the comparison against the neurons it replaces.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Sparse autoencoder** — An autoencoder trained to reconstruct with a sparse code.
- **Dictionary feature** — A feature found by a sparse autoencoder.
- **L0** — The number of features that are active.
- **Explained variance** — How much of the activation the reconstruction accounts for.

*Read first:* Polysemanticity

## 3. Patching

*From what a neuron responds to, to what it does*

A correlational claim about a neuron is cheap; a causal one is not. This module covers the intervention that distinguishes them, and the measurement that comes with it.

**Learning outcomes**

- Describe activation patching and what it establishes
- Compute the effect of patching a node, and the normalised effect
- Define the faithfulness of a proposed circuit

### Lesson 5. Activation patching

*The intervention that makes a claim causal*

*Estimated study time:* 24 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Describe activation patching and what it establishes
- Compute the effect of patching a node and the normalised effect
- Explain why a self-consistent model is not an explanation

**The ideas**

- Run the model twice, and replace one activation in one of the runs.
- If the output moves, that node was causally responsible for the move.
- Correlational evidence survives the patch; causal evidence does not.

#### Practice

**Q. What does activation patching establish? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **That a node is causally responsible for a change in the output**
- That a node responds to a particular input
- That the model has understood the input
- That a node is important

> Correct.

> **Why:** You run the model twice, replace one activation in one of the runs, and look at what moves. If the output changes, the node was responsible for it.

**Q. A model with a perfect self-consistency score can still be wrong about what it is doing. — boolean *(hard)***

> **Answer:** True

> **Why:** Yes. Self-consistency is a correlational property; a model can be perfectly self-consistent and implement a mechanism that does not explain the behaviour.

#### Go and do it

Patch each node in turn and read the effect on the output. Open **Patch a node** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §circuits:2.3 Step 3: Patch model activations to isolate the relevant subgraph · p. 3 — The intervention, and what it rules out.
- §sae:4 Identifying Causally-Important Dictionary Features · p. 8 — Adapting the patching procedure to dictionary features.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Activation patching** — Run the model twice, and replace one activation in one of the runs.
- **Causal** — A claim that survives an intervention.
- **Attribution** — How much a component is responsible for the output.

*Read first:* Polysemanticity

## 4. Circuits

*An explanation that accounts for the behaviour*

The workflow the circuit-discovery paper lays out: choose a behaviour, divide the model into components, find the ones that matter, and explain them. This module puts the pieces in order and says what each one buys.

**Learning outcomes**

- State the four steps of the mechanistic-interpretability workflow
- Explain what a node, an edge and a path are in a transformer
- Argue for a behavioural explanation over a correlational one
- Split one head’s QK and OV circuits, and one pathway into the terms that make it up
- Say what an automated circuit search is scored against, and what it can get wrong

### Lesson 6. The workflow

*Four steps, and what each one is for*

*Estimated study time:* 20 minutes

**What you will learn**

- State the four steps of the mechanistic-interpretability workflow
- Say what a node, an edge and a path are in a transformer
- Argue for a behavioural explanation over a correlational one

**The ideas**

- Choose a behaviour, divide the model into a graph, patch, and explain.
- A node is a component that does one thing; an edge is a causal influence.
- A finished explanation accounts for the behaviour, not for a correlation.

#### Practice

**Q. What are the four steps of the mechanistic-interpretability workflow? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **Select a behaviour, divide the model into a graph, patch to isolate the subgraph, and explain the components**
- Collect data, train a probe, read the probe, write it up
- Find the neurons, find the features, find the data, find the answer
- Prune, retrain, compare, publish

> Correct.

> **Why:** The order matters: a behaviour first, so that the explanation is of something the model actually does.

**Q. In a transformer, what is the natural unit of a circuit node? — multiple-choice *(hard)***

- ✓ **An attention head or a feed-forward block, reading from and writing to the residual stream**
- A single weight
- A whole layer
- A training example

> Correct.

> **Why:** The natural decomposition is the one the architecture gives you: the components that write to the residual stream, and the causal influences between them.

#### Go and do it

The graph of nodes and edges, with the attribution on each. Open **The circuit** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §circuits:2 The Mechanistic Interpretability Workflow · p. 2 — The four steps, in order, and why each one is needed.
- §circuits:2.2 Step 2: Divide the neural network into a graph of smaller units · p. 3 — The graph, and the vocabulary of components.
- §circuits:2.4 Explaining the circuit components · p. 4 — What a finished explanation has to contain.

- [A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework.html) — The residual stream, the nodes, the edges and the paths.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Circuit** — A graph of components that accounts for a behaviour.
- **Node** — A component of the graph that does one thing.
- **Path** — A chain of causal influences from an input to the output.
- **Faithfulness** — How much of the effect a proposed subgraph accounts for.

*Read first:* Activation patching

### Lesson 9. The QK and OV circuits

*One head, two matrices, and an exact split of what it contributes*

*Estimated study time:* 24 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Factor one attention head into the circuit that chooses a position and the circuit that writes from it
- State the pathway decomposition of a last-layer head and why it is an identity rather than an approximation
- Explain why a head in an earlier layer has no such split, and what can be measured instead
- Describe what path patching asks that component patching cannot

**The ideas**

- A head is four matrices and two products: W_QᵀW_K decides where it looks, W_OW_V decides what it writes when it gets there.
- A last-layer head’s effect on a logit difference is exactly the sum over source positions of attention times the write that position is worth — so the decomposition can be checked against an ablation to machine precision.
- A composed head’s QK circuit is a property of the path into it, which is why the induction circuit cannot be read off either head alone.

#### Practice

**Q. What does a head’s QK circuit decide, and what does its OV circuit decide? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **QK decides which positions the head looks at; OV decides what it writes once it has looked**
- QK decides the layer, OV decides the head
- QK decides what is written, OV decides what is attended to
- Both describe the attention pattern, in different bases

> Correct.

> **Why:** W_Qᵀ W_K and W_O W_V are two separate d_model × d_model products that factor out of the head, and that factorisation is what lets you patch a head through one circuit input of another head instead of through the head as a whole.

**Q. Splitting a last-layer head’s effect on the metric into per-position terms is an approximation that leaves a few percent unexplained. — boolean *(hard)***

> **Answer:** False

> **Why:** No. The head’s output is a sum over source positions and the readout is linear, so the split is an identity: in the laboratory the sum of the terms equals the ablation’s effect and the discrepancy column is driven below 1e-12 by a test. A head in an *earlier* layer has no such split, because its effect runs through the softmax of the layer above.

#### Go and do it

Pick a head and a position, and read the head’s whole contribution as one term per source position, next to the ablation that has to equal it. Open **Decompose a pathway** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §framework:1 The Residual Stream · p. 1 — The computational graph a transformer induces, and the factorisation of a head into a QK and an OV circuit.
- §induction:reverse-engineering Summary of Reverse Engineering Induction Heads · p. 26 — The composed circuit those two circuits are read in, on a model whose wiring is known.

**Further reading**

- [A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework.html) — The QK/OV vocabulary, the path expansion, and the composition of heads.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Residual stream** — The vector every component reads from and writes to.
- **QK circuit** — The product W_Qᵀ W_K, which decides which positions a head attends to.
- **OV circuit** — The product W_O W_V, which decides what a head writes for the positions it attends to.
- **Path** — A chain of causal influences from an input to the output.
- **Path patching** — Patching one head’s output into a single circuit input of another head.

*Read first:* The workflow, Induction heads

### Lesson 10. Automating the search

*Edge attribution, pruning, and what a discovered circuit is graded against*

*Estimated study time:* 22 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Define the attribution score of an edge and say why it is marginal rather than intrinsic
- Describe the prune-and-rescore loop and the threshold it stops at
- State faithfulness and completeness as two different failures
- Explain why a hand-wired circuit is the only honest ground truth for a discovery algorithm

**The ideas**

- An edge’s score is what the current graph loses when that edge is deleted, so an edge can look essential only because its partner is in the graph — which is why the search re-scores everything at every step.
- A graph can be faithful without being complete, or complete without being faithful: one names a route that carries the behaviour on its own, the other names everything the behaviour cannot do without.
- On a random model the strongest available claim is that the numbers are self-consistent. On a model wired by hand the search’s answer is a test.

#### Practice

**Q. Why does an ACDC-style search re-score every remaining edge at every step? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **Because an edge’s score is its contribution to the graph it is currently in, so deleting one edge changes what the others are worth**
- Because the metric is stochastic and needs averaging
- Because the model is retrained between steps
- Because scores have to increase monotonically

> Correct.

> **Why:** A key path and the query path that reads it only work together: each looks essential while both are present, and one becomes free the moment the other goes. A single ranking would delete the wrong edge first.

**Q. A pruned graph that is faithful but not complete names every component the behaviour depends on. — boolean *(hard)***

> **Answer:** False

> **Why:** No. Faithfulness says the graph reproduces the behaviour on its own; completeness says nothing outside it is needed. A faithful-but-incomplete graph is an explanation that still leans on a component it has never named — which is why the two criteria are reported as a pair.

#### Go and do it

Score every edge, delete the weakest, and watch faithfulness and completeness fall — then compare what the search reports against the four edges the wiring needs, from two different corruptions. Open **Prune a graph down to a circuit** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §circuits:3 Automating circuit discovery (Step 3) · p. 3 — The attribution-patching loop, its cost, and the threshold it stops at.
- §circuits:4 Evaluating Subgraph Recovery Algorithms · p. 9 — How a discovery method is scored — against a hand-built circuit, on tasks where the answer is known.

**Further reading**

- [Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997) — ACDC, and the two criteria the pruned graphs are graded on.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Circuit** — A graph of components that accounts for a behaviour.
- **Node** — A component of the graph that does one thing.
- **Edge attribution** — One edge’s marginal contribution to the graph that currently contains it.
- **Faithfulness** — How much of the effect a proposed subgraph accounts for.
- **ACDC** — The search that deletes the least-scored component until the graph stops being faithful.
- **Completeness** — How much of a behaviour the circuit reproduces.

*Read first:* The workflow, The QK and OV circuits

## 5. Composition

*One head shifts the keys; another completes the pattern*

A single attention head can only match what is written at a position. Most of what a transformer does happens because one head’s output becomes another head’s input. This module builds the clearest example — the induction circuit — and then the largest hand-built circuit in the literature, where the same logic is followed through a whole model.

**Learning outcomes**

- Describe the two-head induction circuit and what each head contributes
- Measure the accuracy of the composed circuit, and the effect of removing its first head
- Explain completeness and minimality as tests of a circuit, not of a story

### Lesson 7. Induction heads

*The smallest circuit that is more than one head*

*Estimated study time:* 26 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Describe the induction algorithm: [A][B] … [A] predicts [B]
- Explain what the previous-token head contributes to the second head
- Measure the accuracy of the composed circuit, and of the ablation

**The ideas**

- An induction head matches the current token against the token that came before each earlier position, then copies the token after the match.
- The previous-token head is what shifts the keys: without it, the second head can only find the current token itself.
- The paper’s causal test is an ablation, and in the laboratory the ablation takes the accuracy to zero while the fixed circuit is exact.

#### Practice

**Q. What does the previous-token head contribute to the induction circuit? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **It shifts the keys, so the second head can match the current token against what came before each position**
- It copies the answer token into the output
- It suppresses the wrong answer
- It decides when to stop attending

> Correct.

> **Why:** The first head writes each token’s predecessor into the position’s key. The induction head then matches the current token against that shifted content; without the shift, it can only find the current token itself.

**Q. An induction head with no previous-token head can still find the token that followed the previous occurrence. — boolean *(hard)***

> **Answer:** False

> **Why:** Without the shift, its keys are the tokens themselves, so it matches the earlier occurrence of the current token and copies that token — not the one that followed it. The laboratory’s ablation measures exactly this collapse.

#### Go and do it

A hand-wired two-head circuit on a repeated sequence, with both attention patterns and the ablation. Open **Complete the pattern** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §induction:key-concepts Key Concepts: In-context Learning and Induction Heads · p. 4 — The [A][B] … [A] definition, and the two heads that implement it.
- §induction:reverse-engineering Summary of Reverse Engineering Induction Heads · p. 26 — The mechanism stated as a circuit: shifted keys, matched queries, copied values.
- §induction:phase-change Looking at the Phase Change More Closely · p. 13 — Induction heads forming at the same moment in-context learning appears.

**Further reading**

- [In-context Learning and Induction Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11895) — The six lines of evidence, of which the ablation is the causal one.
- [A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework.html) — The composition of heads that makes the circuit possible.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Induction head** — A head that completes a pattern it has already seen.
- **Previous-token head** — A head whose attention is on the position before it.
- **Composition** — One head’s output used as another head’s input.
- **In-context learning** — Learning a pattern from the context, without changing a weight.

*Read first:* The workflow

### Lesson 8. The IOI circuit

*A whole behaviour, reverse-engineered*

*Estimated study time:* 26 minutes

**What you will learn**

- Explain how the name-mover heads and the S-inhibition heads divide the work
- Say what completeness and minimality measure, and why both are needed
- Describe what the circuit leaves unexplained

**The ideas**

- The circuit has 26 attention heads in seven classes: some move the name, and some decide which name is moved.
- Completeness asks how much of the behaviour the circuit accounts for; minimality asks whether every part of it is needed.
- The paper’s own evaluation finds the explanation supported and incomplete at the same time — which is what an honest circuit looks like.

#### Practice

**Q. What does minimality measure about a proposed circuit? — multiple-choice *(core)***

- ✓ **Whether every component in it is needed for the behaviour**
- Whether it explains the whole behaviour
- Whether it is smaller than a baseline circuit
- Whether its components are attention heads

> Correct.

> **Why:** Minimality removes components and checks the behaviour survives. Completeness asks how much is explained; minimality asks whether each part is doing work.

**Q. A circuit that passes completeness and minimality is therefore a complete account of how the model does the task. — boolean *(hard)***

> **Answer:** False

> **Why:** No. The paper reports its explanation as supported by both criteria and still incomplete: the criteria constrain the circuit, they do not prove that nothing else is involved.

#### Go and do it

The paper’s own procedure — direct effects, then path patches into the movers’ circuits, then one layer down, then the two criteria — run on a hand-wired circuit with four heads, on the paper’s prompt and on the mirrored one. Open **Run the four steps** in the mech-interp-lab application.

**Where this came from**

- §ioi:3.1 Which heads directly affect the output? (Name Mover Heads) · p. 5 — The heads that write the answer, found by ablating heads one at a time.
- §ioi:3.2 Which heads affect the Name Mover Heads’ attention? (S-Inhibition Heads) · p. 6 — The upstream heads that decide which name is copied.
- §ioi:4.1 Completeness · p. 9 — How much of the behaviour the circuit reproduces.
- §ioi:4.2 Minimality · p. 10 — Whether every component in the circuit is doing necessary work.

**Further reading**

- [Interpretability in the Wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00593) — The 26-head circuit, and the three criteria it is evaluated by.
- [Towards Automated Circuit Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997) — The automated procedure that this circuit was a target for.

**The words this lesson uses**

- **Name-mover head** — The head that writes the answer name into the output.
- **S-inhibition head** — The head that suppresses the wrong name.
- **Completeness** — How much of a behaviour the circuit reproduces.
- **Minimality** — Whether every part of a circuit is needed.

*Read first:* Induction heads

## Appendix A — Glossary

**Superposition** — Several features packed into one direction of the model’s activation.

When a model has fewer dimensions than the features it represents, it cannot give each feature a direction of its own. It packs them together instead, and the features interfere.

*Cunningham et al. (2023)*

**Interference** — The cost two features pay for sharing a direction.

The cross term in the loss, (w_i·w_j)², weighted by the importance of the feature that pays it. It is zero for orthogonal directions and grows quadratically as they align.

*Course term*

**Importance** — How much a feature matters to the loss.

A weight on each feature’s squared error. The toy model assumes the importances follow a power law: a few features matter and a long tail does not.

*Cunningham et al. (2023)*

**Polysemanticity** — A neuron that responds to several unrelated things.

It is the direct consequence of superposition, and it is why you cannot read a model’s computation off its neurons.

*Cunningham et al. (2023)*

**Monosemanticity** — A direction that responds to one thing and nothing else.

The property a good dictionary feature has, and the one the interpretability scoring measures.

*Cunningham et al. (2023)*

**Feature** — A thing the model represents, as distinct from the neuron it uses.

A feature is a direction in activation space that corresponds to something the model can talk about. It need not be a neuron, and in a superposed model it usually is not.

*Cunningham et al. (2023)*

**Dictionary feature** — A feature found by a sparse autoencoder.

One element of the overcomplete dictionary the autoencoder learns. It is a candidate answer to "what is this model representing?".

*Cunningham et al. (2023)*

**Sparse autoencoder** — An autoencoder trained to reconstruct with a sparse code.

f = ReLU(W_enc(x − b_pre) + b_enc), x̂ = W_dec f + b_pre, with the loss ‖x − x̂‖² + λ‖f‖₁. The L1 term is what makes the code sparse, and the sparsity is what makes the features interpretable.

*Cunningham et al. (2023)*

**L0** — The number of features that are active.

The count of non-zero entries in the code. It is the sparsity the penalty buys, and the smaller it is the more interpretable the dictionary tends to be.

*Course term*

**Explained variance** — How much of the activation the reconstruction accounts for.

One minus the reconstruction error, divided by the variance of the activations. A dictionary that explains the variance has not thrown the information away.

*Course term*

**Activation patching** — Run the model twice, and replace one activation in one of the runs.

If the output changes, the node that was patched was causally responsible for the change. It is the difference between "responds to" and "does".

*Conmy et al. (2023)*

**Causal** — A claim that survives an intervention.

A correlational claim holds over the data you have; a causal claim holds over the data you would have had if you had intervened.

*Course term*

**Attribution** — How much a component is responsible for the output.

The effect of patching it, measured against the largest effect any component could have had.

*Conmy et al. (2023)*

**Circuit** — A graph of components that accounts for a behaviour.

Not a list of the features a model uses, but a small set of components and the causal paths between them that together explain what the model did.

*Conmy et al. (2023)*

**Node** — A component of the graph that does one thing.

In a transformer the natural nodes are the attention heads and the feed-forward blocks, and the natural edges are the causal influences between them.

*Elhage et al. (2021)*

**Path** — A chain of causal influences from an input to the output.

What an explanation is made of: a small number of paths, each of which carries the signal that mattered.

*Elhage et al. (2021)*

**Faithfulness** — How much of the effect a proposed subgraph accounts for.

If a graph of nodes reproduces the output change when patched, it is faithful; the score is the fraction of the effect it explains.

*Conmy et al. (2023)*

**Residual stream** — The vector every component reads from and writes to.

The computational graph a transformer induces is a set of components reading from and writing to this one vector, and it is the graph that a circuit is a subgraph of.

*Elhage et al. (2021)*

**Induction head** — A head that completes a pattern it has already seen.

It matches the current token against the token that preceded each earlier position, attends to the position after the match, and copies that token. [A][B] … [A] becomes [A][B] … [A][B].

*Olsson et al. (2022)*

**Previous-token head** — A head whose attention is on the position before it.

It moves each token one position forward in the residual stream. The induction head reads that shifted content as its keys, which is the whole of the first head’s contribution.

*Olsson et al. (2022)*

**Composition** — One head’s output used as another head’s input.

Heads write to the residual stream, and a later head reads from it. A behaviour that neither head can produce alone can be produced by the two in composition — which is why an explanation has to talk about paths and not just heads.

*Olsson et al. (2022)*

**In-context learning** — Learning a pattern from the context, without changing a weight.

Loss on tokens later in a sequence is lower than loss on tokens earlier in it, because the model can use what it has already read. The induction-head paper argues that much of this is pattern completion by circuits like the one in the laboratory.

*Olsson et al. (2022)*

**Name-mover head** — The head that writes the answer name into the output.

In the IOI circuit, the name movers attend to the two names in the sentence and copy one of them to the final position. Which one they copy is decided upstream.

*Wang et al. (2022)*

**S-inhibition head** — The head that suppresses the wrong name.

It writes a signal that keeps the name movers from copying the subject, so the indirect object wins. It does not write the answer; it decides which of two candidates does.

*Wang et al. (2022)*

**Completeness** — How much of a behaviour the circuit reproduces.

Patch every node in the proposed circuit and measure how much of the behaviour comes back. A complete circuit accounts for the behaviour; an incomplete one leaves a residue it does not explain.

*Wang et al. (2022)*

**Minimality** — Whether every part of a circuit is needed.

Remove components one at a time and see whether the behaviour survives. A circuit can be complete and still contain components that are doing nothing for this behaviour.

*Wang et al. (2022)*

**QK circuit** — The product W_Qᵀ W_K, which decides which positions a head attends to.

One head reads the residual stream through two independent matrices, and this is the one that scores pairs of positions. It is the whole of the head’s where, and because it factorises out of the head it can be measured on its own — which is what makes a composed head’s influence patchable through its key input rather than through the head.

*Elhage et al. (2021)*

**OV circuit** — The product W_O W_V, which decides what a head writes for the positions it attends to.

Attention chooses the sources; W_O W_V chooses what is taken from each of them and written back into the stream. Because the head’s output is a sum over sources, its contribution to a logit splits into one term per position — the attention weight times the OV write projected on the readout — and that split is exact.

*Elhage et al. (2021)*

**Path patching** — Patching one head’s output into a single circuit input of another head.

Activation patching asks whether a component matters. Path patching asks which of its influences mattered: substitute the ablated head’s write into the query, key or value input of the later head, and the difference is that edge’s contribution. It is the tool that turns the framework’s paths into measurements.

*Elhage et al. (2021)*

**Edge attribution** — One edge’s marginal contribution to the graph that currently contains it.

Score an edge by what deleting it costs the graph, with all the other kept edges still in place. The score is a property of the edge *and its neighbours*, not of the edge alone: two edges that only work together each look essential while both are present. That is why a pruning search re-scores every remaining edge at every step.

*Conmy et al. (2023)*

**ACDC** — The search that deletes the least-scored component until the graph stops being faithful.

Given a metric and a behavioural gap: score every remaining node and edge by its marginal contribution, delete the smallest, repeat, and take as the answer the smallest graph that still cleared the threshold. Nothing is trained and no human chooses the components — which is why the method has to be graded on a model whose wiring is already known.

*Conmy et al. (2023)*
